subject: Bounded transformations after non-centered parameterization (i.e. Matt Trick)

messages.author: 6b3aae728cd578f1
messages.subject: Bounded transformations after non-centered parameterization (i.e. Matt Trick)
parts:
Hi all, 

I am posting a new topic, but this question is related to a previous post which I actually wrote most of this comment out in: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/_D6MlTNQZxk/ . I am posting a new topic because I am not sure if older posts will get attention.

The problem I am encountering is this–my colleagues and I have been using a non-centered parameterization to estimate parameters in a hierarchical model. This parameterization follows the form:

real mu_parameter; 
real<lower=0> sigma; 

vector[N] parameter_raw;
vector<lower=0,upper=1>[N] parameter;

for (i in 1:N) {
  parameter[i] <- Phi_approx( mu_parameter + sigma * parameter_raw[i] );
}

mu_parameter  ~ normal(0,1);
sigma         ~ cauchy(0,5); 
parameter_raw ~ normal(0,1);

As you can see, we transform the parameter to [0,1] with the Phi_approx function (the parameters are rates, which justifies this transformation).

Referring back to the post I linked above (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/_D6MlTNQZxk/), this can sometimes lead to bimodal posterior estimates, where the posterior mass is largely clustered around the parameter bounds. Advice in the linked post was assuming that this may be due to the parameter actually being bimodal, but I am not sure this is the case. My reasoning is outlined below.

In summary, I think this issue (bimodality) may be caused by the prior, which is (I think) placing a large mass on the extremes of the parameter bounds after the probit transformation is applied. I have attached code below (plot_priors.R) that can be used to draw samples from the prior distribution for a parameter being sampled in this way. The code can be modified by changing the distribution of the scale parameter from a cauchy to a normal (line 7), and you can also change the other values used in the sampling (e.g. the hyper_sd scale on line 11). Using the same parameterization as in the example code above, I get prior distributions of the form shown in image_1.png (attached). The image shows what the prior looks like both with (left) and without (right) the probit transformation being applied. On the left, you can see that the prior mass is heavily localized around the parameter bounds. On the right, the prior looks like what you would expect (Note that I am "zooming in" by limiting the x axis between -200 and 200, else you cannot see the form). I think this may explain why bimodal posteriors are common when using this type of parameterization? But I could be wrong–I wanted to post here to see what everyone else thinks. 

Interestingly, when the scale parameter on the cauchy distribution is set very low, the prior distribution over the probit transformed space becomes relatively uniform. image_2.png shows an example of the prior when the scale parameter in the cauchy is set to 0.001 as opposed to 5.  

So, I guess my question is now this–what is the best way to approach this problem? Can the scale parameter for the cauchy be set low, or will this not allow for individual level differences in that parameter estimate (in the case of the example code, differences among parameter)? Another potential solution would be to truncate the parameter being estimated so that values under 0.01 and over 0.99 are not allowed (using the code example above; see image_3.png for a visual depiction of the constraint):

 vector<lower=0.01,upper=0.99>[N] parameter;

However, I understand that hard constraints like this are not ideal. I guess the problem then is coming up with a good soft constraint. 

If anyone has information on the best steps to take in this situation, it would be greatly appreciated. Please let me know if anything is unclear. 

Best, 
Nate

messages.subject: Re: Bounded transformations after non-centered parameterization (i.e. Matt Trick)
parts:
Hi Nate, 

I've only had a chance to glance at it quickly, but I did notice one thing: if you know that parameter has a lower bound of zero then you also need to declare parameter_raw with the same lower bound of zero. 

Jonah

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Bounded transformations after non-centered parameterization (i.e. Matt Trick)
parts:
If a in (-inf, inf) then Phi(a) in (0, 1). No need to bound
a below at zero. (inv_logit, the inverse CDF of the logistic
distribution, is a bit more efficient, and is the basis of
the Phi_approx function.)

Usually if there's a problem like this, it's because
the data are pulling your parameters toward the boundary.

I had a hard time following all those things with "parameter"
in the name, but in general, if

y ~ normal(0, 1)

then

Phi(y) ~ uniform(0, 1)

If y ~ normal(0, sigma) for sigma > 1, then it's bimodal at the
extremes, whereas if sigma < 1, then it's unimodal.

Similarly, if

y ~ logistic(0, 1)

then

inv_logit(y) ~ uniform(0, 1)

You can't do what you're trying to do with constraints. What you
can do, but which we don't recommend (because if the data's causing
a pileup near the boundary, moving the boundary will just exacerbate
the problem), is to do this:

0.98 * Phi(y) + 0.01

to generate values in the (0.01, 0.99) range.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Bounded transformations after non-centered parameterization (i.e. Matt Trick)
parts:
Sorry, I read that too quickly. Bob's right that "parameter" is just a deterministic transformation using Phi(_approx) and so is constrained to the unit interval by construction. 

The rest of Bob's advice is good too (as usual).

Jonah
